bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isNonEmptyString` that returns `true` only for strings with at least one non-whitespace character. Signature: `isNonEmptyString(v: unknown): v is string`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Order matters: the typeof check must pass before `.trim()` is safe to call — in TS the && already narrows `v` to string for the second operand. Rejecting whitespace-only strings is the practical definition of "required field" in every form backend.
hints: typeof first, then trim and check the length.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isPositiveInt` that returns `true` only for integers greater than 0 (reject floats, NaN, Infinity, strings). Signature: `isPositiveInt(v: unknown): v is number`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: `Number.isInteger` knocks out floats, NaN, and the infinities in one call (none of them are integers). This is the validator for ids, quantities, page numbers — anywhere "a number" actually means "a counting number".
hints: Three checks chained with &&: typeof, Number.isInteger, > 0.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isStringArray` that returns `true` only for arrays in which EVERY element is a string (an empty array passes). Signature: `isStringArray(v: unknown): v is string[]`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: `every` on an empty array returns true (vacuous truth), which is the right call for "a possibly-empty list of tags". Array.isArray is the container check — typeof reports arrays as "object", as course 1 warned.
hints: Array.isArray, then .every with a typeof check.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isUser` that validates `{ id: number; name: string; email: string }`: object, non-null, correct typeof for all three fields. Extra fields are allowed. Signature: `isUser(obj: unknown): obj is User`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: The single local cast to `Record<string, unknown>` is the accepted idiom: it grants property *access* while every *value* stays unknown and must be typeof-checked. A missing field reads as undefined and fails its typeof — absence and wrong-type are rejected by the same line.
hints: Guard-clause the non-object cases first, then cast ONCE to Record<string, unknown> and check fields.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isProduct` that validates `{ sku: string; priceCents: number; tags: string[] }` — including that `tags` is an array of strings. Signature: `isProduct(obj: unknown): obj is Product`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Validators compose: the tags check is isStringArray embedded in a larger guard. Real schemas are trees of exactly these primitives — which is why schema libraries are combinator libraries, and why hand-rolling a few makes zod’s API instantly familiar.
hints: Compose the isStringArray logic inline for the tags field.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isEmailish` that does a pragmatic email shape check: a string containing exactly one `@`, with a non-empty part before it, and a part after it that contains a `.`. (Real email validation is famously impossible by regex — this is the useful 95%.) Signature: `isEmailish(v: unknown): v is string`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Splitting on `@` and checking for exactly two parts handles both "no @" and "two @s" in one comparison — cleaner than counting. The honest comment in the prompt is part of the lesson: for emails, shape-check cheaply and let the confirmation email be the real validator.
hints: split("@") must yield exactly 2 parts — that simultaneously rejects zero and multiple @s.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isPercent` that accepts only numbers from 0 to 100 inclusive (NaN and non-numbers rejected): `isPercent(50)` → `true`, `isPercent(100.5)` → `false`. Signature: `isPercent(v: unknown): v is number`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: NaN needs no special case here: every comparison with NaN is false, so `NaN >= 0` already rejects it — a rare case of NaN’s weirdness working FOR you. Range checks like this (percentages, ports, latitudes) are the second layer of validation after typeof.
hints: typeof plus two range comparisons. What do those comparisons return for NaN?

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a type guard `isIsoDateString` that checks for a YYYY-MM-DD date string: exactly that shape (regex `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/`), with month 01–12 and day 01–31. `'2026-01-15'` → `true`; `'2026-13-01'`, `'20260115'`, `42` → `false`. Signature: `isIsoDateString(v: unknown): v is string`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Layered validation mirrors how parsers think: cheap structural checks first (typeof, regex), semantic checks second (ranges). A full calendar check (no Feb 30) would use the Date object — but even this 80% version catches the transposed-field bugs (day 32, month 13) that plague date handling.
hints: Three layers: typeof, regex shape, then slice out month/day and range-check them.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `parseUser` that validates like isUser but reports WHAT failed: return `{ ok: true, value }` for a valid `{ id: number; name: string }`, else `{ ok: false, error }` with error `'not an object'`, `'invalid id'`, or `'invalid name'` — first failure wins, checked in that order.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: parse beats is when callers need to answer "why was this rejected?" — a 400 response with "invalid id" saves hours over a bare false. Building the success value as a fresh `{ id, name }` (instead of returning the input) also strips unknown extra fields: parse, don’t validate, as the slogan goes.
hints: Guard clauses in the specified order, each returning its own error; success constructs a CLEAN object.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `parseBool` that parses the strings `'true'` and `'false'` (exactly, case-sensitive) into booleans: return `{ ok: true, value: boolean }`, anything else → `{ ok: false, error: 'expected "true" or "false"' }`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Boolean parsing is a minefield of implicit coercion — `Boolean("false")` is true! An explicit two-literal parser is boring and correct, and the result union keeps "could not parse" distinct from "parsed to false", which a `boolean` return type would conflate.
hints: Two exact comparisons and a fallback error.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `parseIntStrict` that parses a string that is ENTIRELY an optionally-negative integer (regex `/^-?\d+$/` is a good fit): `'42'` → `{ ok: true, value: 42 }`; `'42px'`, `'4.2'`, `''` → `{ ok: false, error: 'not an integer' }`. (Note `Number.parseInt('42px', 10)` would wrongly accept it).
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: `parseInt` stops at the first non-digit ('42px' → 42), which silently accepts garbage — the regex anchors `^` and `$` demand the entire string be digits. Validate the raw string, then convert: separating those steps is what makes the parser strict.
hints: Test the WHOLE string with a regex first, then convert with Number().

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `requireKeys` that returns the sorted list of required keys MISSING from an object (not own properties): `requireKeys({ a: 1 }, ['a', 'b', 'c'])` → `['b', 'c']`. A complete object returns `[]`. Signature: `requireKeys(obj: Record<string, unknown>, required: string[]): string[]`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Reporting ALL missing keys at once beats failing on the first — a user fixing a form wants the complete list, not a fix-resubmit loop. The `{ a: null }` case pins a subtle choice: hasOwn says the key is present even when its value is null; presence and validity are separate questions for a validator.
hints: filter the required list by !Object.hasOwn, then sort.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `checkFieldTypes` that validates an object against a schema of expected typeofs (`{ name: 'string', age: 'number' }`): return a sorted array of error strings — `'<key>: missing'` for absent keys, `'<key>: expected <type>'` for wrong types. Valid object → `[]`. Signature: `checkFieldTypes(obj: Record<string, unknown>, schema: Record<string, string>): string[]`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: A schema as data means one validator serves every shape — this ten-line function is a seed-crystal zod. Driving iteration from the schema (not the object) makes extra input fields harmless and missing ones detectable. Collect-and-sort turns validation into a deterministic, testable pure function.
hints: Drive the loop from the SCHEMA keys; two failure modes per key, collected not thrown.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `cleanRecords` that filters a raw array down to the elements that satisfy `{ id: number; name: string }` (object, non-null, correct field types), returning them in order and SKIPPING the rest. Signature: `cleanRecords(rows: unknown[]): { id: number; name: string }[]`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Skip-the-bad-rows is the pragmatic policy for bulk data — one malformed record should not torpedo an import of thousands (though production code would also COUNT the skips). Rebuilding each accepted row strips stray fields; `rows.filter(isRow)` is the one-liner variant, with the guard’s type predicate making the output type come out right.
hints: Write the guard once, then loop-and-push (or rows.filter(isRow)).

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export a function `parsePort` that parses a TCP port from a string: the string must be entirely digits (regex `/^\d+$/`) AND the number must be 1–65535. Return `{ ok: true, value }`, or `{ ok: false, error: 'not an integer' }` for non-digit strings, or `{ ok: false, error: 'out of range' }` for 0 or > 65535.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: Distinguishing "not a number at all" from "a number, but not a legal port" is the difference between a user fixing a typo and a user hunting a config convention. The 1–65535 range is a real-world domain constraint — the kind of knowledge that belongs IN the parser, once, not sprinkled across callers. You will reuse exactly this in the Node course’s env parsing.
hints: Two distinct failure modes deserve two distinct error strings — shape check, then range check.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions: Export `isArrayOf<T>(guard: (v: unknown) => v is T, value: unknown): value is T[]` — a higher-order validator: it checks that `value` is an array AND that the supplied guard passes for every element. `isArrayOf(isNum, [1, 2])` → true; `isArrayOf(isNum, [1, "2"])` → false; non-arrays → false.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: This is a validator *combinator*: it takes a guard and produces a new guard for arrays of that thing. Passing `guard` straight to `every` works because a type predicate IS a boolean function. One `isArrayOf`, combined with the element guards you wrote earlier, validates `User[]`, `Product[]`, `string[][]`... — composition is how ten small validators cover a hundred shapes.
hints: Array.isArray plus .every(guard) — the guard is already the right callback shape.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.instructions:
Export `parseSettings(input: unknown)` that validates and normalizes app settings. Rules:
- If input is not a non-null object → `{ ok: false, errors: ['not an object'] }`.
- Fields (all optional in the input, all present in the output):
  - `theme`: must be `'light'` or `'dark'` if present (default `'light'`)
  - `fontSize`: must be a number 8–32 if present (default 14)
  - `autosave`: must be a boolean if present (default `true`)
- Collect ALL field errors as `'<field>: invalid'` in field order (theme, fontSize, autosave). Any errors → `{ ok: false, errors }`; otherwise → `{ ok: true, value: { theme, fontSize, autosave } }` with defaults applied for absent fields.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/runtime-valid.explanation: This is the full boundary pattern: validate, collect (never throw-on-first), default, and normalize — the output type has no optional fields, so downstream code never re-checks. The crucial policy the tests enforce: an *invalid* provided value is an error, not a silent fallback to the default — silently "fixing" a typo like fontSize: 99 is how user settings get mysteriously lost. Every config loader you meet (and the next course writes one for env vars) is a variation of exactly this function.
hints: Per field: hasOwn? → validate (collect error or accept); absent → default. Keep a mutable local per field.
Absent and invalid are DIFFERENT: absent gets the default, invalid gets an error — never a silent default.
Only build the success object after checking errors.length.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/qui.instructions: Why map a database row to a DTO instead of returning the row from the API directly?
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/qui.explanation: The mapper is a security boundary and a stability boundary at once: secrets stay in because only listed fields cross, and you can migrate the database without breaking API clients (or vice versa) because the two shapes are linked only through one function you control.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/qui.instructions: What is wrong with `function toDto(row) { return { ...row, id: row.user_id }; }`?
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/qui.explanation: Spreading makes the mapping *opt-out* (fields leak unless removed); constructing field-by-field makes it *opt-in* (fields private unless listed). For data crossing a trust boundary, opt-in is the only safe default — the leak arrives silently with a later migration, which is what makes this bug class nasty.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/qui.instructions: Your database uses snake_case and your frontend camelCase. Where should the conversion happen?
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/qui.explanation: Converting "defensively" everywhere means you can never tell which convention a given object is in — the bugs look like missing fields (`user.createdAt` undefined because this one came through as `created_at`). One boundary, one convention per side, and every layer knows what shape it holds.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/out.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/out.explanation: The DTO contains only the two listed fields — the JSON shows id and name, and the `in` check confirms password_hash never crossed the boundary. The mapper constructs rather than spreads; that is the entire security property.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/sna.instructions: Export a function `snakeToCamel` that converts a snake_case identifier to camelCase: `'created_at'` → `'createdAt'`, `'a_b_c'` → `'aBC'`. Already-camel strings pass through unchanged.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/sna.explanation: The replacer-function form of replace is the key tool: the regex captures the letter after each underscore, and the function returns its upper-cased form, consuming the underscore. The `g` flag handles multiple underscores in one pass.
hints: replace(/_([a-z])/g, fn) — the capture group is the letter after each underscore.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/cam.instructions: Export a function `camelToSnake` that converts camelCase to snake_case: `'createdAt'` → `'created_at'`, `'aBC'` → `'a_b_c'`. Lower-case-only strings pass through.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/cam.explanation: The inverse direction needs no capture group: each capital letter IS the match, replaced by underscore plus its lower-case self. Together with snakeToCamel you now own both directions of the API↔DB boundary.
hints: Replace each capital letter with underscore + its lowercase form.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/key.instructions: Export a function `keysToCamel` that converts the TOP-LEVEL keys of an object from snake_case to camelCase (values untouched): `{ user_id: 1, full_name: 'Ada' }` → `{ userId: 1, fullName: 'Ada' }`. Signature: `keysToCamel(obj: Record<string, unknown>): Record<string, unknown>`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/key.explanation: Lifting the string converter to object keys is one loop. The nested case in the tests pins the "shallow" contract — inner objects keep their keys, which is the honest behavior until you deliberately write the recursive version (this lesson’s challenge).
hints: Loop the keys, write each value under the converted key.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/key.instructions: Export a function `keysToSnake` that converts the top-level keys of an object from camelCase to snake_case (values untouched): `{ userId: 1 }` → `{ user_id: 1 }`. Signature: `keysToSnake(obj: Record<string, unknown>): Record<string, unknown>`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/key.explanation: This is the write path: a camelCase request body becomes a snake_case row for an INSERT. Owning both directions as pure functions makes the boundary testable without a database in sight.
hints: Mirror of keysToCamel with the other string converter.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/keb.instructions: Export a function `kebabToCamel` that converts kebab-case (CSS/URL style) to camelCase: `'font-size'` → `'fontSize'`, `'a-b-c'` → `'aBC'`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/keb.explanation: Same machine, different separator: once you own the replacer-function pattern, every casing convention is a one-character regex change. Kebab-case is what CSS properties and URL slugs use, so this converter sits at the DOM/style boundary the way snakeToCamel sits at the DB boundary.
hints: Identical to snakeToCamel with a dash in the regex instead of an underscore.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/cam.instructions: Export a function `camelToKebab` that converts camelCase to kebab-case: `'fontSize'` → `'font-size'`, `'borderTopWidth'` → `'border-top-width'`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/cam.explanation: The fourth and final converter completes the toolkit: snake↔camel for the API/DB axis, kebab↔camel for the CSS/JS axis. All four are the same two regexes with different separators — recognizing that collapses what looks like four utilities into one idea.
hints: Each capital becomes dash + lowercase.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/to-.instructions: Export a function `toUserDto` that maps a `UserRow` (`{ user_id, full_name, email, password_hash, created_at }`) to a `UserDto` (`{ id, name, email, createdAt }`) — renamed fields, NO password_hash, constructed explicitly (no spread).
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/to-.explanation: The archetypal mapper: rename (user_id → id), pass through (email), convert convention (created_at → createdAt), and omit the secret — all by construction. The declared return type is the safety net: drop a field and the compiler, not a client, tells you.
hints: Four explicit assignments; password_hash simply never appears.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/to-.instructions: Export a function `toProductDto` that maps a product row `{ product_id, display_name, price_cents, internal_cost_cents }` to `{ id, name, price }` where `price` is a display string from cents (e.g. 1999 → `'19.99'` via `(cents / 100).toFixed(2)`) and the internal cost is omitted.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/to-.explanation: Mappers do more than rename — they are the place for representation changes (integer cents → display string) so the rest of the system keeps exact integers. And internal_cost_cents staying private is a business rule, enforced the same way as the password hash: by not writing it.
hints: The mapper is also where unit/format conversion lives: cents → display string.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/map.instructions: Export a function `mapUsers` that applies the user mapping over a whole result set: `mapUsers(rows)` maps each `{ user_id, full_name }` to `{ id, name }`, preserving order. Signature: `mapUsers(rows: { user_id: number; full_name: string }[]): { id: number; name: string }[]`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/map.explanation: List endpoints are single-row mappers lifted with `map` — write the row mapper once, apply it everywhere. The `(row) => ({ ... })` parentheses are the syntax gotcha: without them the braces parse as a function body, not an object.
hints: rows.map with the single-row mapping inline (note the parentheses around the returned object literal).

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/lis.instructions: Export a function `toListResponse` that wraps items in the standard list envelope: `toListResponse(['a', 'b'], 1, 10, 42)` → `{ data: ['a', 'b'], meta: { page: 1, perPage: 10, total: 42, totalPages: 5 } }` where totalPages is `Math.ceil(total / perPage)` (0 when total is 0). Signature: `toListResponse<T>(items: T[], page: number, perPage: number, total: number)`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/lis.explanation: A consistent envelope (`data` + `meta`) means every client pagination component works against every endpoint. The generic `ListResponse<T>` types the envelope once for all resources; `Math.ceil` handles the final partial page (7 items at 3 per page = 3 pages).
hints: Math.ceil(total / perPage) — check it gives 0 for total 0 and rounds 7/3 up to 3.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/err.instructions: Export a function `errorBody` that builds the standard error envelope: `errorBody(404, 'Not Found', '/users/9')` → `{ error: { code: 404, message: 'Not Found', path: '/users/9' } }`. Signature: `errorBody(code: number, message: string, path: string)`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/err.explanation: Trivial to write, valuable to standardize: when every failure returns the same shape, clients write ONE error handler. The nesting under `error` leaves room for the envelope to grow (requestId, details array) without breaking existing consumers.
hints: Nest the three params under an error key — shorthand properties do the rest.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/par.instructions: Export a function `parseSortParam` that parses an API sort query value: `'name'` → `{ field: 'name', dir: 'asc' }`, `'-created_at'` (leading minus) → `{ field: 'created_at', dir: 'desc' }`, and empty string → `null`. Signature: `parseSortParam(raw: string): { field: string; dir: 'asc' | 'desc' } | null`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/par.explanation: The `-field` convention (borrowed from JSON:API) packs direction into one query param; parsing it into a typed `{ field, dir }` object at the boundary means the query-builder layer never string-matches again. The bare "-" guard is the kind of degenerate input fuzzers (and users) find immediately.
hints: startsWith("-") decides the direction; slice(1) strips the prefix. Guard the degenerate inputs first.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/to-.instructions: Export a function `toOrderDto` that maps an order row `{ order_id, user_id, total_cents, status, internal_notes }` to `{ id, userId, total, status }` where `total` is the display string from cents (`(cents / 100).toFixed(2)`) and internal_notes never leaves.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/to-.explanation: A second mapper to cement the moves: rename (order_id → id), case-convert (user_id → userId), represent (cents → display string), pass through (status), omit (internal_notes). Every mapper you ever write is some combination of these five verbs.
hints: Rename, convert the money representation, pass status through, omit the notes.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/api.instructions: Export a function `apiOk` that wraps a successful payload in the standard success envelope: `apiOk({ id: 1 })` → `{ data: { id: 1 }, error: null }`. Signature: `apiOk<T>(data: T): { data: T; error: null }`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/api.explanation: The success twin of errorBody: `{ data, error: null }` and `{ data: null, error: {...} }` give clients one unconditional shape to destructure. The literal type `error: null` (not `string | null`) tells TypeScript consumers that checking `error` truly discriminates the two envelopes.
hints: One object literal; the generic keeps the payload typed.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/bui.instructions: Export a function `buildPatch` that sanitizes a PATCH request body: keep only the keys listed in `allowed` that are actually present on the input (own properties), dropping everything else — `buildPatch({ name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }, ['name', 'email'])` → `{ name: 'Ada' }`. Signature: `buildPatch(input: Record<string, unknown>, allowed: string[]): Record<string, unknown>`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/bui.explanation: This is `pick` wearing a security hat: an allowlist over a request body is what stops a client from PATCHing `role: "admin"` onto their own account (a mass-assignment vulnerability — the Rails world learned it the hard way). The `email: null` case matters: null is a legitimate "clear this field" patch and must survive, which is why the check is hasOwn, not truthiness.
hints: It is pick, reframed: iterate the ALLOWLIST, copy only what exists.

bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/dee.instructions: Export `deepKeysToCamel(value: unknown): unknown` — the recursive version of keysToCamel. Rules: plain objects get their keys converted from snake_case AND their values converted recursively; arrays are mapped element-by-element (recursively); everything else (strings, numbers, booleans, null) passes through unchanged. Example: `{ user_id: 1, past_orders: [{ order_id: 9 }] }` → `{ userId: 1, pastOrders: [{ orderId: 9 }] }`.
bootforge/ts-apps/modeling/api-types/dee.explanation: Recursive structure transformation has exactly three cases, and their ORDER is the exercise: arrays before objects (arrays pass the typeof-object test), null excluded from the object branch (the eternal `typeof null` trap), primitives as the base case. String values are deliberately untouched — only *keys* convert, which the `"still_snake"` test pins. This function, pointed at every API response, is how whole SDKs normalize third-party payloads in one place.
hints: Order of checks matters: arrays ARE objects, so test Array.isArray first.
The object branch does two jobs per key: convert the key, recurse on the value.
The base case is "anything else": return it untouched — that includes null (which typeof calls object!).
